summary: Teach natural selection in insects (ages 9-11) using the peppered moth: adaptation arises across MANY GENERATIONS as selection acts on EXISTING variation in a population, NOT by an individual changing within its lifetime. The load-bearing goal is to confront the Lamarckian error ('the moth turned dark because of the soot / because it needed to') by showing that it is which moths survive and breed that changes, not the moths themselves. A generation-by-generation selection model (toggling sooty vs clean environments and tracking the colour ratio, with a 'follow one moth' probe) is intended to make the mechanism visible; discussion, sequencing, and matching activities extend and check it; a static before/after scene is a useful scaffold with the limit that it cannot show the generational shift unfolding.
misconceptions: 'The moth turned dark because of the soot / because it needed to' — the Lamarckian error; individuals don't change to fit.
'Adaptation happens within one insect's lifetime' — it occurs across generations.
'The moths chose to camouflage' — selection is not a conscious decision.
'The environment creates the new trait' — variation pre-exists; the environment selects among it.
'Evolution has a goal / strives toward perfection' — it's differential survival and reproduction, not purpose.

activities.title: Run the generational selection model: watch the population shift, not the individual
steps: Start with a pale-lichen tree and a moth population that is mostly light with a few dark moths (variation that already exists).

Each round, let a bird eat the moths it can most easily SEE; on the pale tree the dark moths stand out and are eaten, the survivors breed, and read the colour ratio off a live population graph as the next generation appears.
Slide the environment into the Industrial Revolution so soot blackens the bark; now the LIGHT moths are the visible ones. Run several more generations and watch the graph flip toward mostly dark.
Slide the air clean again and run more generations to watch the ratio reverse back toward pale.
Use a 'follow one moth' tag on a single individual across the rounds and confirm it NEVER changes colour — only which moths survive to breed changes.
State in your own words what changed: the population's mix of colours, not any single moth's colour.
activities.insight: Adaptation is selection acting on pre-existing variation across generations: better-camouflaged individuals survive and leave more offspring, so the population's trait frequency shifts. An adult moth's inherited wing colour stays the same for its whole adult life.

activities.title: Explain the reversal and transfer to other animals (stick insects and ant-mimicking spiders)
steps: Explain, in writing or aloud, why pale moths became common again after air pollution fell (for example through clean-air laws) and trees got cleaner — using survival of existing variants, not moths changing themselves.
Answer: 'Could ONE adult moth, in its own life, change its wing colour from pale to dark to hide better? So what actually changed — the moth, or the population?'
Apply the same reasoning to a stick insect: did one stick insect grow twiggy on purpose, or did twig-like ones survive better over generations? Explain using differential survival and inheritance.
Apply it again to ant-mimicking spiders: explain how looking like an ant could help an individual survive and pass on that appearance.
activities.insight: The same mechanism — differential survival of pre-existing variation, inherited across generations — explains the reversal and generalises to many camouflage and mimicry adaptations; it is not a one-off story about moths.

activities.title: Socratic discussion to surface and correct the Lamarckian idea
steps: Discuss the question 'Did the moth decide to change colour?' and defend your answer.
Respond to follow-ups that probe intention and timescale, e.g. 'Did the moths change because they needed to?' and 'Did this happen to one group of moths in a single summer?'
Restate the mechanism without using words like 'turned', 'changed to fit', or 'adapted itself'.
activities.insight: Natural selection is a filter acting on variation, not a conscious choice or a need-driven transformation, and it unfolds over many generations rather than within one lifetime.

activities.title: Check understanding: sequence, contrast, and match
steps: Order the peppered-moth events into the correct selection story (clean trees with mostly pale moths → soot darkens bark → dark moths better hidden → dark survivors breed more → population becomes mostly dark → clean air returns → pale moths favoured again).
Answer a contrasting question: 'Did the moth turn dark, or did dark moths survive better?' and justify the choice.

Match each animal to the function of its adaptation (stick insect's twig shape → hide from predators; ant-mimicking spider's ant-like look → fool predators; peppered moth's dark colouring on sooty bark → camouflage). Note that the spider is an arachnid, not an insect.
activities.insight: Consolidate the distinction between individual change and population shift, and connect adaptations to the survival function they serve.

activities.title: Read the before/after habitat scene (scaffold)
steps: Study a two-panel scene — an industrial sooty tree and a recovered clean tree — each with its moth population.
Tap or point to reveal which moths are easiest for a predator to see in each panel.
Describe which colour is better hidden in each environment and predict which would survive more there.
activities.insight: Camouflage depends on the match between the moth's colour and its background, which sets up why selection favours different colours in different environments.

checkQuestion: During the Industrial Revolution, tree trunks near factories got covered in dark soot, and over time dark peppered moths became far more common than pale ones. A child explains it like this: 'The pale moths turned dark to hide on the sooty trees.' Is that the right explanation? Tell me what actually happened, and why.
checkAnswer: It's not right — individual pale moths did NOT turn dark. What happened is natural selection over generations: moths already varied (some pale, some dark). On sooty trees the dark moths were better camouflaged, so more of them survived and had young; pale moths were spotted and eaten more. So over many generations the dark colour became common — the POPULATION changed because the survivors passed on their colour, not because any single moth changed itself.
